text:
Retrospective cohort study (PLOS ONE, DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0252158) examining the association between time in the target blood glucose range of 70 to 180 mg/dL and 28-day mortality among patients admitted to the intensive care unit.

BACKGROUND: Glycemic control in critical illness has shifted away from intensive insulin therapy. The landmark NICE-SUGAR randomized trial demonstrated higher mortality with intensive insulin therapy, so current recommendations use less tight control: the American Diabetes Association recommends a target glucose range of 140 to 180 mg/dL for most critically ill patients (grade A), and the Surviving Sepsis Campaign suggests an upper limit of 180 mg/dL. Beyond mean glucose, the proportion of time spent within the target range (TIR) has emerged as a prognostic marker.

FINDINGS: Earlier work showed that a TIR of 70 to 140 mg/dL below 80% was associated with higher mortality in non-diabetic critically ill patients with HbA1c of 6.5% or less. This study tested TIR 70 to 180 mg/dL against 28-day mortality in ICU patients, hypothesising that lower time-in-range predicts higher mortality risk. The analysis supports TIR as an independent prognostic factor in critical care, complementing mean glucose and hypoglycaemia avoidance.

PRACTICAL IMPLICATIONS: For most critically ill adults, aim for blood glucose 140 to 180 mg/dL and avoid both hyperglycaemia and hypoglycaemia; protocols typically use intravenous insulin infusions with frequent point-of-care monitoring (every 1 to 2 hours in unstable patients). Maximizing the proportion of readings within 70 to 180 mg/dL, rather than chasing normoglycaemia, is the evidence-aligned strategy. Stress hyperglycaemia indices (such as the stress hyperglycaemia ratio) are emerging as additional risk-stratification tools, particularly in patients with chronic kidney disease.
title: Time in blood glucose range 70-180 mg/dL and survival in critically ill patients
